verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Tinsukia tea estates with processing assets and diversified revenue; avoid single-garden, erosion-exposed, wage-sensitive borrowers until cash-flow and land-loss risks are verified.
title: Tinsukia Tea Plantations: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A tea estate turns standing leaf into made tea, and cash comes from auction and private sales weeks after plucking.** Green leaf is plucked, withered, rolled, fermented, dried and sorted in the estate's own factory; the crop is seasonal, so working capital peaks in the plucking months and unwinds through the year. **Value sits in the factory and the bush age profile, not in the land alone** — ICRA notes one peer's favourable bush age (around 82% in the 6-50 year group in FY2026) drove a yield of 2,370 kg/hectare [8]. Capex is replanting, factory machinery and worker housing; pricing power is thin because made tea is a commodity, so margin is a cost game. **Ask every borrower for their cost of production per kg and their own yield per hectare — collect from customer.**

## What has changed now
**Two local facts matter more than the national tea story.** Brahmaputra erosion is threatening the Rungagora and Dinjan tea estates in Tinsukia, with the local MLA calling for anti-erosion measures [2] — that is a direct asset-loss risk, not a sentiment issue. Separately, a Tinsukia estate has become the first in India to produce Matcha commercially [3], which shows a premium-product route exists but is early and unproven at scale. **Assam's electricity demand grew only 1.9% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5% [D], a local stress signal, while GST collections grew 36.9% against India's 6.1% [D].** Peer results are mixed: one plantation company swung to a Q1FY27 net profit of Rs 115.52 lakhs from a Q4FY26 loss of Rs 581.93 lakhs, yet sales de-grew [6].

## Where to grow
**Pursue estates with their own factory, a young bush profile and a second revenue line.** The peer evidence is clear: aerospace components earn 20-30% EBITDA margins versus 5-10% for tea [4], and carbon-credit potential from estate forest cover is a future non-tea income [4]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower has a factory, a buyer linkage and any diversification; if the answer is only green-leaf sale to others, ask for the buyer contracts and price history.** Avoid gardens sitting on eroding river frontage [2] and single-garden borrowers with no processing asset.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the crop cycle, not the balance sheet date.** Sanction working capital sized to peak plucking months, with a cash-flow statement by month; take stock and book-debt statements every month, and a factory utilisation report quarterly. **Take the land and factory as primary security and a personal guarantee; if the borrower's yield or bush age is unknown, ask for the replanting register before enhancing limits.** For premium-product proposals like the Matcha line [3], lend only against confirmed offtake, not against the idea.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the garden, the wage bill and the buyer list.** If erosion reports name the borrower's estate [2], freeze enhancements and re-verify the mortgaged land. If monthly stock statements show made tea piling up unsold, ask for the auction invoices. If sales de-grow while profit jumps, as in the peer case [6], ask what one-off item drove the profit. **Tinsukia-specific published data is thin — the sources say little about this city beyond the erosion and Matcha items, so lean on first principles and peer numbers.**
watch: Made tea inventory rising two months running -> ask for auction invoices and cut limit utilisation
Erosion report names borrower's garden -> freeze enhancements and re-verify mortgage
Sales de-grow while profit jumps -> ask for one-off items behind the profit
Utilisation falling below plan -> review working capital cycle and buyer contracts
Cost per kg rising without price pass-through -> reprice or reduce exposure
